speaker: fitz
text: In 1978, this tower's structural engineer found a hidden weakness. He believed a strong enough storm could break it.

speaker: gauge
text: A fifty-nine-story skyscraper. Standing on four stilts, in the middle of each side.

speaker: gauge
text: I've cracked it already. They ran out of money and forgot the corners.

speaker: fitz
text: Not quite. The corners are open on purpose.

speaker: gauge
text: And nobody noticed the weakness?

speaker: fitz
text: The full story stayed hidden for almost seventeen years.

speaker: gauge
text: A secret skyscraper? Get the red string. All of it.

speaker: fitz
text: Gauge, why are you tied to the lamp?

speaker: gauge
text: Everything's connected, Fitz. Especially me and this lamp.

speaker: fitz
text: This is Citicorp Center in Manhattan, finished in 1977, more than nine hundred feet tall. Its engineer was William LeMessurier.

speaker: fitz
text: The stilts come first. One corner of the block belonged to Saint Peter's Lutheran Church.

speaker: gauge
text: Theory two. The corners didn't run out of money. The church took them.

speaker: fitz
text: Half right. One corner. The church kept its corner, and got a brand new building on that corner, with the tower rising over it. So no column could stand there.

speaker: fitz
text: The four big columns went to the middle of each side instead. The corners hang out about seventy-two feet, with nothing underneath.

speaker: gauge
text: That's like a table with the legs in the wrong place.

speaker: fitz
text: It would be, without the braces. Behind the glass are steel braces, eight stories tall, in upside-down V shapes. They steer the weight and the wind from the corners down into those four columns.

speaker: gauge
text: Secret V shapes. Pinning it. Pinning it twice.

speaker: fitz
text: The frame was light. About twenty-five thousand tons of steel, less than half the Empire State Building's.

speaker: gauge
text: Light is good. Light is fast. Light is... wobbly?

speaker: fitz
text: Exactly. A light tower sways more in the wind. So near the top, LeMessurier added something special.

speaker: fitz
text: A concrete block of about four hundred tons, riding on a thin film of oil. When the tower sways one way, the block is pushed the other way.

speaker: fitz
text: Think of a passenger on a swaying train who always leans the other way.

speaker: fitz
text: It cuts the sway by up to about half. It's called a tuned mass damper, and it was one of the first in a skyscraper.

speaker: gauge
text: A giant concrete block, surfing on oil. I love him. I'm naming him Kevin.

speaker: fitz
text: Please don't name the damper. But remember this: it was built for comfort, so people wouldn't feel the building move. Not to hold it up. And it needed electricity to work.

speaker: gauge
text: Comfort. Needs power. Kevin needs a plug. Pinning it.

speaker: fitz
text: Hold onto that one. It matters later.

speaker: gauge
text: Fitz, I pinned a sandwich. I don't know why. It felt like a clue.

speaker: fitz
text: That's your lunch.

speaker: fitz
text: Here's how LeMessurier told the story. In June 1978, his office got a phone call from an engineering student in New Jersey. The student's professor wanted to know why the columns weren't at the corners.

speaker: gauge
text: The professor agrees with me. The corners. Forgot. Them.

speaker: fitz
text: LeMessurier explained the columns were placed to handle wind from every direction, even wind hitting a corner.

speaker: fitz
text: Engineers call that a quartering wind. It hits at an angle and pushes on two sides at once.

speaker: gauge
text: So it's like getting hit by two snowballs at the same time, right on the elbow.

speaker: fitz
text: That's... actually a decent picture of it.

speaker: fitz
text: Back then, New York's building code only asked engineers to check winds that hit a side straight on. LeMessurier thought the tower would make a good lesson for his engineering class. So he checked corner winds himself.

speaker: fitz
text: In some of the big V-shaped braces, a corner wind raised the force by about forty percent.

speaker: gauge
text: Forty percent! Case closed. The braces were too weak. Somebody get me a tiny judge's hammer.

speaker: fitz
text: No. The braces themselves were strong enough. The question was how they were joined together.

speaker: fitz
text: On paper, the joints were welded, which is very strong. But that May, at a meeting about a different building, LeMessurier had learned something about this one.

speaker: fitz
text: The joints hadn't been welded. They'd been bolted.

speaker: gauge
text: Plot twist. Pinning it. In red. I'm out of red. I'm using spaghetti.

speaker: fitz
text: Back in 1974, the steel company suggested bolts instead of welds, to save money. His firm's New York office agreed.

speaker: gauge
text: So bolts are the villain?

speaker: fitz
text: No, bolts are normal and safe. The problem was what these were designed to hold.

speaker: fitz
text: They were sized for straight-on winds only. And the braces had been counted as parts of a truss, not as columns, which left out a safety margin the rules required. So there were fewer bolts than there should have been.

speaker: gauge
text: How does forty percent turn into a problem for a bolt?

speaker: fitz
text: Picture a tug of war. The wind pulls the joint apart. The building's own weight pushes it back together. The joint only has to hold the difference. And the weight never changes.

speaker: gauge
text: So the weight is the big kid at the back of the rope who refuses to move.

speaker: fitz
text: Exactly. So when the wind's pull grew by forty percent, the leftover pull on the joints grew far more. LeMessurier worked it out at about one hundred and sixty percent.

speaker: gauge
text: The tug-of-war math is not on our side. I'd like to switch teams.

speaker: fitz
text: The wind tunnel lab in Canada that had tested the tower re-ran the numbers. Real storms shake a building, so the loads could be higher still.

speaker: fitz
text: The weakest joint was at the thirtieth floor. He estimated how often a storm strong enough to break it comes along.

speaker: gauge
text: And? How often?

speaker: fitz
text: With the damper off, about a one in sixteen chance in any year.

speaker: gauge
text: One in sixteen. So it's safe for fifteen years? I did math.

speaker: fitz
text: You did math wrong. It's a one in sixteen chance every single year. With the damper running, he estimated about one in fifty-five.

speaker: gauge
text: Kevin! Kevin can save the day.

speaker: fitz
text: Only if he has power. And a big storm can knock the power out.

speaker: gauge
text: Of course it can. Kevin, I'm so sorry.

speaker: fitz
text: LeMessurier later said, "I had information that nobody else in the world had." It was late July.

speaker: gauge
text: What do you do with information like that?

speaker: fitz
text: That's the next question. And it's a hard one.

speaker: fitz
text: He could have kept quiet. Instead, he told his insurance company, the architect, and then the bank's leaders.

speaker: gauge
text: Worst meeting ever. "Hi, it's your engineer. Quick question about your tower."

speaker: fitz
text: Within days, there was a plan. Steel plates about two inches thick would be welded over more than two hundred bolted joints.

speaker: gauge
text: Like a bandage. A very heavy bandage. A two-inch bandage.

speaker: fitz
text: The welders worked at night, from about eight in the evening to four in the morning, seven days a week. Each joint was boxed in plywood, and by morning people came to work as usual.

speaker: gauge
text: So it's a heist movie. Except they break in at night to add steel.

speaker: fitz
text: That was the idea. Emergency generators kept the damper running, and weather experts watched for storms.

speaker: gauge
text: Kevin got a generator. Good for Kevin.

speaker: fitz
text: And quietly, the bank, the city, the police and the Red Cross planned how to evacuate the tower and the neighborhood around it, if a dangerous storm came.

speaker: gauge
text: What did they tell the public?

speaker: fitz
text: On August eighth, the bank announced the joints would be strengthened. It said the engineers had assured it there was no danger.

speaker: gauge
text: "No danger." Pinning that one. With a question mark. And a smaller question mark.

speaker: fitz
text: The next day, a strike shut the city's big newspapers for nearly three months. The real reason never made the front pages.

speaker: gauge
text: Talk about timing.

speaker: fitz
text: Then, at the start of September, a hurricane named Ella was moving north off the East Coast.

speaker: gauge
text: Tell me it didn't get close. Fitz. Tell me.

speaker: fitz
text: The storm records show Ella stayed hundreds of miles out over the ocean, then turned away.

speaker: gauge
text: Thank you, Ella.

speaker: fitz
text: The welders fixed the most critical joints first, and finished in October. LeMessurier estimated the tower could now handle a seven-hundred-year storm, even without the damper.

speaker: gauge
text: From one in sixteen to one in seven hundred. I'd take that trade. Kevin can finally relax.

speaker: fitz
text: Two million dollars was paid to the bank through LeMessurier's insurance, with no lawsuit. And then, the story went quiet.

speaker: gauge
text: Almost seventeen years quiet? I can't keep a secret for seventeen seconds.

speaker: fitz
text: And when it finally came out, the famous version wasn't quite what happened.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1995, the writer Joe Morgenstern told the full story in The New Yorker. It became famous. But parts of the famous version don't hold up.

speaker: gauge
text: Myth check. I made a stamp. It says "myth." It also says "Gauge," because I couldn't fit it all.

speaker: fitz
text: Myth one: a Princeton student found the flaw.

speaker: fitz
text: There was a Princeton student, Diane Hartley. Her 1978 senior thesis studied this tower, and her numbers suggested corner winds raised the stresses.

speaker: fitz
text: She raised it with an engineer at his New York office, never with LeMessurier himself. She learned about the crisis years later, from a TV show.

speaker: gauge
text: So was she the caller?

speaker: fitz
text: Nobody knows for sure. Another student, Lee DeCarolis, later said he made the call. He says he was passing on his professor's questions about the columns.

speaker: gauge
text: Two students, one phone call. I'm going to need more spaghetti.

speaker: fitz
text: And neither student knew about the bolts. LeMessurier found that problem himself.

speaker: gauge
text: So it's not "a student found it." It's "students asked good questions."

speaker: fitz
text: Exactly. Myth two: the tower was about to fall down.

speaker: gauge
text: That's the one I believed. I've had the stamp ready since the cold open.

speaker: fitz
text: That one in sixteen was LeMessurier's estimate in 1978. Decades later, researchers at the U.S. government's measurement lab took another look, with modern methods.

speaker: fitz
text: Using a similar building, they found that straight-on winds, not corner winds, were the bigger load. So the danger from corner winds may have been overestimated.

speaker: gauge
text: Wait. So it was fine all along? I wasted so much spaghetti.

speaker: fitz
text: We can't say that either. The bolts were still short on their safety margin. What we know is that the repair made the tower much stronger.

speaker: gauge
text: Myth three. Kevin was holding the building up.

speaker: fitz
text: No. It was built for comfort. In 1978 it was only a backup, and only while the power stayed on.

speaker: gauge
text: Kevin is a comfort block. That's still a very important job.

speaker: fitz
text: Today the tower is called six-oh-one Lexington Avenue. In 2016 it became an official New York City landmark, and it's still full of offices.

speaker: fitz
text: Engineering students study it in ethics classes, and LeMessurier is widely praised for coming forward about his own firm's mistake.

speaker: fitz
text: But hard questions remain. The public was told there was no danger. Should people have been told more?

speaker: gauge
text: And which student really made that phone call?

speaker: fitz
text: And how close did it really come? Honest answer: people still disagree.

speaker: gauge
text: Final theory. They didn't forget the corners. The corners were the whole point.

speaker: fitz
text: That's the first theory you've had that I'd pin.

speaker: gauge
text: So the case is closed, but the questions are still open.

speaker: gauge
text: Also, I've known this secret for a whole episode and told no one. New record.

speaker: fitz
text: You're telling everyone right now.

speaker: fitz
text: If you want to see how a damper like that works, we made a Short about skyscraper dampers.

speaker: gauge
text: Ooh, what else is built weird? Subscribe and let's find out.
